title: Ahead: thinkers and practices
hookLine: year four reads the Tao Te Ching, Montaigne, Emerson and Thoreau, and studies the science and schools of practice
last: A DOOR YOU KNOW THE LOCATION OF.

lines: A READING LIST ON THE FRIDGE.
cards: Next year's reading list is short enough to tape to the fridge: a small old book of short chapters from China, a Frenchman writing about himself, and two Americans from the same town, one giving lectures, one building a cabin by a pond.
Below them, a stack of studies on what quiet attention does to a person, and a row of doors marked Zen, Sufi, Jewish, Christian contemplative, Sikh, and more.
Year four changes the shape: fewer voices, read slowly, and then the practice itself, looked at closely. Today, a look at what's ahead.

teach.h: THE TAO TE CHING, ONE CHAPTER AT A TIME.
teach.b: First, the Tao Te Ching, one chapter at a time. It's a short Chinese classic, some chapters only a few lines long, and it keeps praising what most people overlook.
Water, it says, does good to everything and settles in the low places nobody wants. The empty space inside a bowl is what makes the bowl useful. Second, Montaigne.

teach.h: MONTAIGNE: I AM THE MATTER OF MY BOOK.
teach.b: In his note to the reader at the front of his Essays, he says that he himself is the matter of his book. No grand subject: one man, his habits, moods and fears, looked at honestly.
He tries out a thought, turns it over, and isn't embarrassed to change his mind.
Third, Emerson and Thoreau. Emerson, in his essay Self-Reliance, wrote: "Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string."

His friend Thoreau went to live by Walden Pond, and wrote: "I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately." One wrote about trusting the inner voice; the other went to the pond to try living by his.
Fourth, the science and the schools. Year four studies what researchers can honestly say about attention, habit and compassion, including what the studies don't show.

Then it visits the world's schools of practice, each in its own home: Zen and Theravada, Tibetan Buddhism, Christian contemplatives, Jewish, Muslim and Sufi, Hindu, Sikh and Chinese ways, and modern secular ones.
At the end, how to choose a practice, and how to respect the ones you don't choose. Year three asked what life is for. Year four asks how people have actually trained themselves to live it.

how: Some people who follow a reading path look over the coming year's books before they start, and pick one they are most curious about to give them something to look forward to.

practice: Let the list go past: the old Chinese book, the Frenchman, the lecturer, the man at the pond, the studies, the schools.
Notice which one your attention leans toward, the way you lean toward a window when someone says look, and name it. If nothing leans, that's fine: the first chapter begins either way.
